expected_findings.description: `PartialEq` is now case-insensitive while `Hash` is still derived over the raw `String`, so two `Tag`s that compare equal can hash differently. That violates the `Hash`/`Eq` contract the standard library requires of `HashSet` keys, and `TagSet` stores `Tag` in a `HashSet` a few lines below. `TagSet::contains` misses a tag that was inserted under a different capitalisation, and `TagSet::insert` reports such a tag as new and stores a second copy, so the set holds entries its own `PartialEq` calls duplicates.

notes:
Constructed by replacing a derived `PartialEq` with a hand-written case-insensitive one while leaving the derived `Hash` in place. rustc does not diagnose this (clippy's `derived_hash_with_manual_eq` would, but the crate builds warning-free under plain `cargo test`).

Why the existing tests miss it: the change added `tags_compare_without_regard_to_case`, which tests `Tag` equality directly and passes, so the suite looks like it covers the new behaviour. Every `TagSet` test, however, uses a single spelling throughout - `inserting_the_same_tag_twice_is_a_no_op` inserts "release" twice, `an_inserted_tag_is_found` looks up the exact string it inserted, and `distinct_tags_are_all_kept` uses two tags that differ in more than case. No test crosses the two halves by inserting one capitalisation and looking up another, which is the only way the inconsistency becomes visible.

Verified by execution: a throwaway integration test (deleted afterwards) printed:
  a == b : true
  hash(a) == hash(b) : false
  contains("release") after inserting "Release" : false
  insert("release") reported as new : true
  set len : 2
with a = Tag::new("Release"), b = Tag::new("release"), hashed with DefaultHasher.

also_accept covers Correctness (lookups return the answer the type's own equality contradicts) and StateManagement (the set accumulates duplicate entries).
